title: Mamo! Tato! · zwroty
note: James's spine decision #4: vocative stays CHUNK-LANE ONLY, never opened as a case, no endings rule stated anywhere in the pack. Six frozen calling-forms, each handed over as a memorized whole exactly like mogłby/mogłaby were in b1_polite: mama->Mamo!, tata->Tato!, babcia->Babciu!, dziadek->Dziadku! (all four verified NEW via check_new before writing), plus two panie/pani + name chunks named in the spine text itself: Panie Piotrze! and Pani Anno! (piotr/anna already GLUE names in audit.py; their inflected calling-forms Piotrze/Anno are new strings, taught here as one more frozen whole, same treatment). SCOPE CUT, logged: the name-vocative pattern itself is NOT generalised to any other name and no rule connecting Piotr->Piotrze or Anna->Anno is stated anywhere in the pack - a productive proper-noun vocative rule would be a second alternation stacked on top of the family-word set in the same unit, which the spine's own 'never taught as a case, no endings rule' line already forecloses; if James wants a general name-vocative unit later, nothing here blocks it, but it is not on the current B1-SPINE as its own slot. Every combination sentence recycles a b1_polite/A1/A2 frame in full (dziękuję za prezent, chciałbym zapytać, gdzie jest dworzec, jak się masz, wszystko dobrze, czy mogłaby pani mi pomóc, czy mógłby pan mi pomóc, przepraszam że przeszkadzam) - checked individually via check_new.py, all confirmed already taught, none touched or altered.

intro.title: A special voice for calling someone
intro.body: When you call out directly to someone in Polish, some words change shape — not to say something ABOUT the person, just to call them. This is a small closed set. Learn each one whole, exactly as it stands. There is no rule to build from — just six words to remember, the same way you learned mógłby and mogłaby as whole blocks.
intro.body_pl: Wołacz: forma wołania. Zapamiętaj całe słowo — bez reguły.

intro.title: Formal address: panie/pani + name
intro.body:
Two more calling-forms, this time formal — panie for a man, pani for a woman, in front of the first name. The name changes shape too, but you never need to work out how: take each one whole, exactly as given.

Panie Piotrze! — calling out to a man named Piotr, formally.
Pani Anno! — calling out to a woman named Anna, formally.

These are the only two names this course teaches the calling-form for. It does not generalise to other names.
intro.body_pl: Panie Piotrze! Pani Anno! — całe zwroty, bez reguły.

examples.en: Mr. Piotr! Excuse me, could you help me?
examples.pl: Panie Piotrze! Przepraszam, czy mógłby pan mi pomóc?

examples.en: Ms. Anna! Thank you very much!

intro.title: Putting it at the front of a sentence you already own
intro.title_pl: Na początku zdania, które już znasz
intro.body: The calling-word goes first, then any sentence you already have.

quiz.prompt: You want your mom's attention. You say:
quiz.explain: Mamo is the special calling-form — a different word from plain mama, used only to call out to her.
Only the calling-form Mamo opens a sentence this way — the other three are the plain, possessive-object and genitive forms you already know.

quiz.prompt: Addressing a man named Piotr, formally:
quiz.explain: This whole phrase — panie, not pan, and Piotrze, not Piotr — is memorized as one block. Nothing here is built from a rule.

quiz.prompt: Addressing a woman named Anna, formally:
Przepraszam, ___, czy mógłby pan mi pomóc? (to Piotr)
quiz.explain: The formal calling-form comes before the request, exactly as pan/pani already do in Czy mógłby pan…?
Głodny agrees with the speaker, not with dziadek — a man speaking says głodny, a woman speaking would say głodna.
